newsitem.title: UK: UK's wise men seek rate rise to restrain demand.
newsitem.headline: UK's wise men seek rate rise to restrain demand.

text.p: The UK Treasury's panel of independent economic advisers warned the Chancellor on Thursday he would have to raise interest rates further as his 1997/98 budget will fail to rein in accelerating consumer demand. "The implied growth rates of domestic demand are for five percent a year, unless something else happens, which does amount effectively to boom rates of growth," Tim Congdon, director of Lombard Street Research, told the House of Commons Treasury Select Committee.
Congdon and fellow "wise man" Gavyn Davies, said Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's budget did not do enough to subdue an increasingly spendthrift British public.

"Demand is now growing too rapidly," said Davies, who is Goldman Sachs' chief economist. "We're getting lots of information from the monetary indicators and the labour market...that demand may grow very rapidly next year, more rapidly than the Treasury is forecasting."
"The implication of my...remarks is that interest rates have to go up further," he said.

Clarke raised UK interest rates by a quarter point at the end of October to 6.0 percent. He now faces the dilemma of whether to risk alienating an already critical British electorate by raising rates again before the general election.
Clarke faced a difficult task in this year's budget, juggling market calls for fiscal tightening with pressure from edgy backbench MPs to deliver vote-winning tax cuts.

He settled on what he termed a prudent budget, delivering a one penny cut in the basic rate of personal income tax to 23 pence, slightly more than offset by spending cuts and revenue raising initiatives.
One of the strands to his revenue-raising plan was a "spend to save package" to crack down on benefit fraud -- a policy Davies said did not stand up to scrutiny.

"You really have to put a big question mark over the 'spend to save' package," he said. "It wouldn't be too cynical to suggest that...the Treasury has been unable to get public spending in its genuine sense down to within the target limits it set itself and has therefore invented these fraud packages in order to get public spending down."

Clarke said in his budget speech that he would put an end to "some of the clever wheezes" dreamed up to avoid paying Value Added Tax. The overall package would cost 800 million stg over three years but recoup 6.7 billion stg, he forecast.
Davies found that hard to believe. "My best guess is that the (budget) package will be modestly restrictive, not as restrictive as it appears from the Red Book," he said.

Wise man Patrick Minford challenged Davies over his sceptical assessment of the state of Britain's public finances. "The longer-term financial situation is much better than Gavyn Davies has painted it. That implies...there was the scope in this budget to cut marginal tax rates much more," he said.
"The fundamental finances of the public sector...are as sound as in the whole of the OECD, if you do the sums looking forward and including pensions."
Minford, who has repeatedly called for lower interest rates and lower taxes, said the view Britain was on the verge of an unsustainable boom was "fanciful".
He pointed out Britain already had the highest real interest rates in Europe by a large margin.
A further tightening of monetary policy would be "highly inappropriate for an economy which has got a great deal of excess capacity in the labour market," Minford said.
